title: used to, would, be used to, get used to
tagline: Past habits that stopped, present habits that feel normal, and the change between them.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Part 1 — talking about your past and how things have changed
Writing Part 2 — article or story about change
why: Four very similar-looking forms mean three different things, and B2 First loves testing exactly that confusion: used to talks about the past, be used to talks about the present, and mixing them up in Part 4 changes whether a habit is finished, current, or still becoming normal.

diagrams.title: A habit that stopped

marks.label: He doesn't play chess any more.

diagrams.caption: Liam used to play chess every lunchtime, but he stopped when he joined the football team.

diagrams.title: Three different ideas, three different forms

rows.label: used to + infinitive
cells: a past habit or state, now finished
I used to walk to school.

rows.label: would + infinitive
cells: a repeated past action (not a state)

rows.label: be used to + -ing
cells: familiar with something now, it feels normal
I'm used to the noise now.

rows.label: get used to + -ing
cells: the process of becoming familiar with something
I'm getting used to the heat.

diagrams.title: be used to vs get used to

parts.ex: I'm getting used to the noise

diagrams.caption: Both are followed by a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive — this is the error the exam checks most often.

head: Form
Pattern
Time
Example
rows: used to
used to + infinitive
past habit or state, now finished
We used to live near the coast.
would
would + infinitive
past repeated action (no states)
My grandad would tell us stories every evening.
be used to
am/is/are used to + noun/-ing
present — familiar, feels normal
Nadia's used to studying in a noisy house.
get used to
am/is/are getting used to + noun/-ing
present — in the process of adapting
I'm still getting used to the new timetable.
Negative
didn't use to / isn't used to
past habit that didn't happen / not familiar
He didn't use to like vegetables.
Question
Did … use to …? / Are … used to …?
asking about a past habit / present familiarity
Did you use to walk to school?

use.point: Past habits and states that have finished

examples.text: Sofia used to be terrified of public speaking.
We used to spend every summer with our cousins in Arequipa.
Mateo didn't use to care about football, but now he never misses a match.
Every Friday, Miss Vega would read us a chapter before the bell went.
examples.note: a repeated action, not a state

examples.text: My dad would always check the score before saying goodnight.
examples.note: a habitual routine, told as a memory

examples.text: Liam is used to getting up at five for training.
examples.note: familiar with it now, it feels normal

examples.text: After three years here, we're completely used to the mountain weather.
I'm not used to speaking in front of the whole school.

use.point: The process of adapting — get used to

examples.text: Nadia is getting used to her new school, though it took her a while.
It took my parents months to get used to living in the city.
examples.note: the process, described in the past

examples.text: You'll soon get used to waking up early for the trip.

watch_out.wrong: I use to play chess every day.
watch_out.right: I used to play chess every day.
watch_out.why: Used to is always spelled with -d, even though it's pronounced like use to.

watch_out.wrong: I am used to get up early now.
watch_out.right: I'm used to getting up early now.
watch_out.why: Be used to takes a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: When I was young, I would be scared of the dark.
watch_out.right: When I was young, I used to be scared of the dark.
watch_out.why: Would doesn't work with states like be, have or like — use used to instead.

watch_out.wrong: She didn't used to like coffee.
watch_out.why: In the negative and question forms, use to loses the -d because did already carries the past.

watch_out.wrong: He is getting used to lived in a new country.
watch_out.right: He's getting used to living in a new country.
watch_out.why: Get used to also needs a noun or -ing form, not an infinitive.

dialogue.title: New house, new routine
dialogue.context: Nadia has just moved to a new neighbourhood in Lima. Sofia and Mateo are asking how she's settling in.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: So how's the new house? Are you used to it yet?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Slowly. I'm still getting used to the traffic noise — my old street was so quiet.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I remember when we moved. I didn't use to sleep well for the first month.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Exactly! And my dad used to drive me everywhere, but now I 'm used to taking the bus alone.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's a big change. What about the neighbours — friendly?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Very. There's an old man who would wave at everyone from his balcony every single morning.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We used to have a neighbour like that too — she would bring us bread on Sundays.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: That sounds lovely. Honestly, I think I'm finally getting used to the whole area.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Give it time. You'll be completely used to it before the school year ends.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I hope so — I really used to miss the sea from my old flat.

items.sentence: When I was small, I ___ afraid of dogs.
items.why: a past state → used to, not would

items.sentence: Every summer, my grandmother ___ take us fishing at dawn.
items.why: a repeated past action (not a state) → would

items.sentence: It took Liam weeks to ___ the new gym schedule.
items.why: the process of adapting → get used to

items.sentence: Mateo ___ studying with music on — he can't concentrate without it.
items.why: a present, familiar habit → be used to

items.sentence: We ___ live in Trujillo before we moved to Lima.
items.why: a finished past state → used to

items.sentence: ___ you use to walk to school when you were younger?
items.why: question form → did + subject + use to

items.sentence: She's still not ___ the cold weather up in the mountains.
items.why: be used to + noun, negative form

items.sentence: He didn't ___ enjoy reading, but now he's always got a book with him.
items.why: negative past habit → didn't use to

summary: Used to + infinitive: a past habit or state that isn't true any more.
Would + infinitive: a repeated past action, told as a memory — never for states like be or like.
Be used to + noun/-ing: familiar with something now, in the present.
Get used to + noun/-ing: the process of becoming familiar with something.
In negatives and questions, used to loses its -d: didn't use to, did you use to…?
